review.title: Religion Review
review.scope: A source-led core review integrating the original Session 1 lecture/transcript, the earlier 40-item paper, a new 100-item compilation and two reordered 20-item papers. All 180 source occurrences are accounted for; repeated questions are not counted as unique content. Added theology, biography, scripture comparison and qualified ethics teaching is distinguished from unverified answer keys, historical reports and an unconfirmed current syllabus.
gaps: Only Session 1 lecture/recording is available; later teaching and the current official syllabus remain unverified.
The papers contain contradictory keys, overlapping alternatives and confessional interpretations. Source marks are not official-key certification.
D19 does not name its three stages. Several reported traditions, D79’s proposer and Bucaille’s claimed conversion remain explicitly qualified.
The exact jurist and classroom edition behind the medical-ethics items are unknown; named current rulings are comparison references, not clinical/legal instructions.
Shomali’s book is lecture-listed and has broad curriculum overlap, but its complete text was not verified as the source of particular items.

modules.title: Lexical and terminological definitions

blocks.text: A lexical definition explains a word through its ordinary meanings, origin and historical use. A terminological definition states the particular meaning used within a discipline or argument. The lecturer explicitly prioritizes the terminological distinction. A historical root does not by itself establish the full doctrinal meaning of a religion.

rows: Lexical
What has this word meant and where does it come from?
Dictionaries, roots and historical usage
Terminological
What exactly does this course or field mean by the term?
A stipulated or technical meaning within the present discussion

blocks.title: Etymology needs caution
blocks.text: Slide 9 links din with obedience and mentions Aramaic, Avestan and Sanskrit. Its English wording is ambiguous and the transcript is unreliable here. Preserve this as the lecturer's claim, not a verified history of all religions.

blocks.question: Why can two definitions of religion differ without one simply being a dictionary error?
blocks.answer: They may select different defining features or use the word at different levels: historical usage, inner experience, belief, moral relationship or a complete normative program.

modules.title: The four introductory interpretations

rows: Creator and associated instructions

Belief in a creator of humanity and the world, with accompanying prescriptions. The slide says scientific instructions; Yazdi Lesson 1 instead describes prescribed actions. Study the practical/normative meaning, not a claim that these are laboratory-science instructions.
Khashiat
An inward reverent state, combining awareness of God with respectful fear.
Goodness throughout existence
Religion as a search for the full meaning of goodness across life.
Living God and moral relationship
Belief in divine will and mind governing the world and morally related to humanity.

blocks.text: These are presented as alternative introductory descriptions. The recording says their purpose is introduction, rather than necessarily memorizing every sentence. Distinguish that teaching comment from the final assessment requirements, which were not supplied.

blocks.title: Academic framing
blocks.text: These notes describe the course's religious framework. They do not present theological assertions as empirical scientific conclusions.

modules.title: The course definition of din

blocks.text: Within the slide's Islamic theological account, din is a divinely designed program intended to guide humanity toward enduring happiness. Its argument connects the creator's knowledge of human nature with the suitability of divine guidance. Explain the reasoning as the course presents it: purpose of human existence, knowledge of that purpose, and a system of guidance suited to it.

blocks.question: How is this definition broader than defining religion as a private feeling?
blocks.answer: It includes a normative program and a human purpose, not only an inward state. The comparison concerns the definitions' scope, not a scientific demonstration that one belief system is true.

modules.title: Beliefs, practice and the structure of religion

references.title: New Religion question paper (highlighted choices, provenance unconfirmed)

blocks.text: A definition first sets the scope of a discussion. In Yazdi’s technical usage, belief in a Creator distinguishes a religious outlook, and the practices prescribed in association with that belief are also included. This broad classification can include beliefs the author considers mistaken. “Religious” therefore does not, by definition alone, mean “theologically correct.” It is not a universal sociological test for classifying every tradition.

rows: Worldview
What is reality? What are humanity, its origin and its destination?
A list of individual ritual instructions.
Ideology
What general pattern of conduct follows from those beliefs?
An unrelated competing explanation of the universe.
Usul (principles)
Foundational religious beliefs.
Only practical duties.
Furu (branches)
Practical rules grounded in those beliefs.
A second creator or independent source of belief.

blocks.text: The examination mapping is worldview to principles, and ideology to general practical branches. The book also allows overlap in usage and applies these words to nonreligious systems. Thus Q4 does not justify saying that worldview and ideology never overlap, or that only religious people have a worldview.

rows: Tawhid - divine unity
Who is the Creator?
Divine justice (adl) is treated as an implication of the first principle, although separately listed in some teaching schemes.
Nubuwwah - prophethood
Where does revealed guidance come from?
Imamah is a particular doctrine concerning continuation of leadership, not one of this question’s shared three.
Ma’ad - resurrection/recompense
What is the ultimate destination and accountability?
The life to come is connected with present beliefs and actions.

blocks.title: Three versus five is a scope question
blocks.text: For Q5, choose imamah as NOT one of the three common fundamentals listed in the text. Do not generalize that answer into “imamah is unimportant” or “justice is denied.” The list changes with the level of classification.

The author’s account begins with original monotheistic guidance and explains later distortion through following desire against that guidance. This is the Islamic theological account tested in Q6, not a demonstrated consensus among historians of religion.

blocks.question: Can a system be religious under the book’s definition while containing beliefs the author rejects?
blocks.answer: Yes. Classification by Creator-belief does not establish the truth of every associated belief. Definition, evaluation and evidence are separate steps.

blocks.question: If a stem asks about behavior rather than the origin and end of humanity, which side of the structure is it testing?
blocks.answer: Usually ideology or practical branches, rather than the worldview or fundamental-belief side. Read whether the question concerns general rules or a particular action.

modules.title: Why investigate? Curiosity, desire and avoidance

references.title: New Religion question paper (highlighted choices, provenance unconfirmed)

blocks.text: Fitrah in the opening inquiry argument is the human disposition to ask and seek understanding. Its initial role is curiosity, not a complete innate knowledge of every doctrine, prophet or ritual. Curiosity opens the question; investigation still has work to do.

rows: Curiosity
Motivates inquiry into origin, purpose and destiny.
Confusing the urge to know with already knowing the answer.
Desire for benefit
May motivate someone to investigate religion if they see possible benefit rather than loss.
Calling all desire irrelevant or necessarily an obstacle.
Desire overriding evidence
Can make a person resist guidance or inconvenient conclusions.
Assuming the positive and negative uses of desire contradict each other.
Apathy / laziness
Avoids undertaking the investigation.
Treating lack of effort as a completed argument.
Fear of restrictions
Avoids finding out because the answer might require change.
Confusing dislike of a conclusion with a refutation.
Expectation of futility
Assumes the inquiry cannot produce a worthwhile result.
Failing to examine that assumption itself.

blocks.text: The sick-child/bitter-medicine analogy targets avoidance of a potentially beneficial investigation because of feared inconvenience. It does not establish that every critic or nonbeliever is irrational. In Q10, rational rejection is the option NOT included in this particular list of avoidance motives; the wording is not a claim that reasoned disagreement cannot occur.
The probability-and-benefit argument

A probability is not the same as the value of its outcome. In the book’s finite commercial illustration, a 5% chance of 1,000 monetary units has a probability-weighted value of 50, while a 10% chance of 100 gives 10. The larger chance does not necessarily identify the more valuable prospect. The comparison holds other costs and conditions aside; it is an illustration, not a complete decision rule.

rows: 1. A possibility is considered
Religious claims might concern enduring happiness or loss.
2. Stakes matter as well as likelihood
A small likelihood is not automatically negligible when the proposed consequence is immense.
3. Proposed conclusion
It is worth investigating those claims seriously.
4. Separate task
Inquiry must still assess whether the claims are true and what follows from them.

blocks.title: Motivation is not proof
blocks.text: Q12 tests the value of investigating the possibility of eternal benefit. It does not prove a 100% success rate, guaranteed material profit, or the truth of a particular creed. The finite arithmetic illustrates sensitivity to stakes; it does not settle every philosophical difficulty about infinite outcomes.

blocks.question: How can desires both encourage inquiry and distort religion?
blocks.answer: Seeking possible benefit can get inquiry started. Refusing evidence because it frustrates a desire can corrupt its outcome. The direction in which desire influences reasoning is the difference.

blocks.question: A student says “this topic may limit my freedom, therefore its claims must be false.” What is wrong with the inference?
blocks.answer: An unwelcome consequence is not evidence of falsity. The book identifies this as a reason someone may avoid inquiry, not as a successful evaluation of the claim.

blocks.question: Why does the 5% versus 10% example not favor the larger percentage automatically?
blocks.answer: Because expected benefit also depends on the magnitude of the outcome. With the stated amounts, 0.05 x 1,000 = 50, whereas 0.10 x 100 = 10.

modules.title: Benefits of religion: purpose, support and responsibility
modules.basis: Learning synthesis from paper; exact prose source not located

references.title: New Religion question paper (highlighted choices, provenance unconfirmed)

blocks.text: This cluster uses section titles such as Sense of Support and Religion and Responsibility that were not securely traced to the inspected Yazdi lessons or to a later local lecture. Learn the conceptual pattern below as a synthesis of the paper. Do not cite it as a newly recovered lecturer transcript or assign an unverified chapter of Shomali’s book.

rows: Hereafter benefit
Present beliefs and actions matter for the life to come; this is ranked as the fundamental benefit.
Not a claim that worldly benefits do not exist, or that rituals alone guarantee success.
Sense of support
The believer regards God as a continuing source of help in distress.
Not a command to reject family, community or practical help.
Self-esteem / dignity
Asking other people for help need not destroy one’s dignity.
Not superiority over others, embarrassment, or never asking for help.
Inner guardian
A felt responsibility before God can regulate conduct even when nobody is watching.
Distinct from police surveillance, social status and immediate public praise.
External deterrence
Fear of a legal penalty may discourage an act when enforcement is expected.
An illustrative mechanism, not a complete account of human morality.

blocks.text: The red-light example contrasts a driver responding only to visible police with a person acting from internal accountability. The generalized distinction is external monitoring versus internalized responsibility. An exam may reverse the example: if the police leave and conduct changes, that illustrates enforcement-dependent deterrence rather than a stable inner constraint.

In Qur’an 6:63-64 the passage first asks about rescue during distress on land and sea, then identifies God as rescuer. The paper’s Q14 selects that rescue motif; Q38 asks for the supporter directly. The same passage also criticizes association of others with God after rescue, but that is not the particular motif Q14 asks you to identify.

blocks.title: Do not turn an exam contrast into a stereotype
blocks.text: Q40’s intended option is fear of punishment within the paper’s simplified contrast. It does not demonstrate that nonreligious people lack conscience, dignity or internal moral commitments. Similarly, a claimed religious benefit is not proof that every believer always behaves well.

blocks.question: An individual maintains dignity while accepting help. Which benefit is being tested?
blocks.answer: Self-esteem, rather than social superiority or refusal of all assistance.

blocks.question: What connects Q15 with Q37, and Q16 with Q40?
blocks.answer: Q15/37 test internal divine responsibility; Q16/40 test the contrasting external-punishment mechanism. The examples differ, but the two mechanisms stay the same.

blocks.question: Why is Hereafter benefit ranked above psychological comfort in this paper?
blocks.answer: The paper places ultimate destiny and accountability above temporary worldly benefits. Explain that hierarchy within the course’s framework, without claiming that comfort or social peace are absent.

modules.title: Taqdir, qada and conditional knowledge records

references.title: New Religion question paper (highlighted choices, provenance unconfirmed)

rows: Taqdir (determination / measure)
Determining characteristics, limits and conditions, including quantity, time and circumstances.
Only a decree concerning human actions; or a synonym that erases all distinction from qada.
Qada (decree / finalization)
An outcome’s realization once its complete conditions are fulfilled.
God waiting to discover a result He did not know.
Epistemic aspect
Divine knowledge of conditions and outcomes.
An event physically occurring merely because a record is being discussed.
Objective aspect
Determination and actualization in the order of created events.
A second, independent universe beyond divine causation.

blocks.text: Q17 compresses the distinction into a gradual, changeable stage versus inevitable fulfillment. B is the intended contrast, but “changeable” belongs to conditioned processes and incomplete descriptions, not to ignorance or revision in God’s complete knowledge. Fulfillment after all conditions are present also does not imply that every natural process has no duration.

headers: How to understand it in this lesson
rows: Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz)
Complete, non-revisable divine knowledge is not made uncertain by human discovery.
Lower / conditional records
An outcome is stated with limited or conditional information; it may change when relevant conditions differ.
Bada’
A change or newly apparent outcome in the conditional order; not God acquiring knowledge that He previously lacked.

blocks.title: Keep the levels separate
blocks.text: If you read “the outcome changed,” ask: changed relative to which conditional record or set of causes? Do not jump from a change in created circumstances to a change from ignorance to knowledge in God.

blocks.question: How can a conditional prediction change without implying divine ignorance?
blocks.answer: The prediction can depend on an incomplete or conditional description, while complete divine knowledge already encompasses the conditions and their outcome.

blocks.question: Which is the safer definition of qada: final actualization under fulfilled conditions, or God guessing the future?
blocks.answer: Final actualization under fulfilled conditions. The second wording contradicts the lesson’s distinction between divine knowledge and events.

modules.title: One act, human choice and divine dependence
modules.basis: Paper Q19-20 + causal distinctions in Lesson 19

references.title: New Religion question paper (highlighted choices, provenance unconfirmed)

blocks.text: The central problem is not merely whether two words can describe the same act. It is how an act can depend upon a human agent and upon God without the two wills canceling one another. The lesson’s answer is dependence at different causal levels: the agent, capacities and exercise of human will do not exist independently of divine causation.

rows: Several contributing causes
Different necessary conditions jointly help produce an event.
Shows that more than one causal contribution is possible.
Successive or mediated causes
One cause operates through another in a chain.
Do not require every cause to be an immediate, competing source.
Hierarchical dependence
A cause and its ability to act depend on a more fundamental cause.
The model used to explain human will within divine causation.
Independent rival wills
Each will would act outside the other’s scope.
This is not the book’s account of divine and human agency.

blocks.text: Study the relationship as: divine sustaining causation -> human agent with capacities and voluntary choice -> chosen act. The arrows mean causal dependence, not a timed sequence in which God first decides and a previously nonexistent human mind is then forced to agree. Human choosing remains part of the account of the voluntary action.

blocks.title: Translation trap: “parallel”
blocks.text: The English reference uses “parallel” but then explains a higher-dependent relation and explicitly rejects a horizontal relation between independent causes. Learn the dependence explained in the paragraph, not that isolated word. Q20’s correct concept is that human will and its existence depend on divine will.

blocks.question: Why does dependence not automatically mean compulsion?
blocks.answer: Dependence concerns the existence and causal power of the agent. Compulsion would deny the voluntary contribution that the account is trying to preserve. They are different claims.

blocks.question: Does “divine decree” justify abandoning effort or responsibility in this lesson?
blocks.answer: No. Voluntary effort is itself among the causes of voluntary outcomes. Treating all human choice as irrelevant removes the very causal element the explanation retains.

modules.title: Prophetic infallibility: scope and agency

references.title: New Religion question paper (highlighted choices, provenance unconfirmed)

blocks.text: Ismah means protectedness or immunity in the relevant scope. The course’s Twelver account is broader than “accurate only while reciting revelation”: it includes protection from sins and from neglect of essential duties, before as well as after the prophetic mission. It does not make every debated question about an ordinary daily lapse identical to a question about sin.

rows: Revelation
Reliable reception, preservation and communication of the message.
A corrupted link would defeat the purpose of reliable guidance.
Moral / obligatory conduct
Protection from sin and omission of essential duties.
Restricting the definition to major sins or only the post-mission period.
Everyday lawful matters
Lesson 25 notes disputed reports and further study regarding ordinary forgetfulness.
Reading this as permission for minor sins, or as proof that revelation may be forgotten incorrectly.
Leaving the better option (tark al-awla)
Not choosing a superior permissible course is distinguished from disobeying an obligation.
Assuming every word of reproach necessarily identifies a forbidden act.
Voluntary agency
Divine help and clear understanding do not erase the ability to choose.
Treating protectedness as an involuntary mechanism with no moral responsibility.

blocks.text: The revelation argument follows the message’s route: divine source -> trustworthy messenger/angel where relevant -> the prophet’s reception and preservation -> faithful transmission to people. A failure within that route would undermine the guidance the route is meant to deliver. This argument directly establishes the need for reliable communication; wider claims about the prophet’s moral example use additional reasoning.

The book describes strong insight into wrongdoing and a firmly developed will, together with divine assistance. As an analogy, knowing that something is poisonous can make voluntary avoidance extremely stable without making a person physically incapable of reaching for it. An analogy clarifies the compatibility claim; it does not independently prove the doctrine.

blocks.title: More help does not mean fewer duties
blocks.text: In the paper’s Q28, greater divinely granted means and attention entail greater responsibility. “No free will,” “exemption from law” and “duties disappear” reverse the intended relationship.

blocks.question: A question permits debate about forgetfulness in an ordinary lawful task. Does that concede prophetic minor sins?
blocks.answer: No. The subject matter has changed: a lawful everyday lapse is not by definition a sin or a failure in communicating revelation. Q25 deliberately tests this scope distinction.

blocks.question: Why can the book regard prophetic good acts as worthy of reward?
blocks.answer: Because the good act remains voluntary. Divine assistance and a stable disposition toward good do not, in this account, turn action into compelled behavior.

blocks.question: Does the scope begin only after appointment as a prophet?
blocks.answer: Not in the Twelver position presented here: protection from sins is extended before the mission as well. Do not confuse that claim with the separate daily-forgetfulness debate.

modules.title: Arguments for infallibility: trust, example and texts

references.title: New Religion question paper (highlighted choices, provenance unconfirmed)

rows: Reliable guidance
Divine wisdom, knowledge and power are invoked to explain protection of the revelation route.
That a prophet must be wealthy, physically strongest, or expert in every worldly science.
Educator and example
One who forms people morally must not undermine that instruction by sinful example.
That mere political power establishes infallibility.
Mukhlas passages
The book cites those purified by God as an exception to Satan’s intended misleading.
That every word for piety has exactly the same grammatical meaning.
Obedience, Qur’an 4:64
Messengers are to be obeyed by God’s leave; the book argues this requires consistency with divine guidance.
That obedience is grounded merely in popular approval.
Mukhlas
One purified or made sincere by God: the protected category intended here.
Mukhlis
One who is sincere: the active description of sincerity.
Muttaqin / muhsinin
The God-conscious / doers of good; related ethical terms, but not the specific tested term.

blocks.text: Lesson 25 develops the mukhlas argument with passages including Sad 38:82-83 and Yusuf 12:24. It also discusses Maryam 19:51 and Sad 38:45-46. Keep the theological interpretation distinct from simply recognizing a verse: the citation supplies wording, and the argument explains how the author uses that wording.

blocks.question: What is added by the educator argument beyond reliable transmission?
blocks.answer: It addresses the prophet as a lived moral example. Reliable words alone would not explain why the guide’s conduct must not contradict the teaching.

blocks.question: Which is the tested wording in 4:64: obey by God’s leave or obey only with popular approval?
blocks.answer: Obey by God’s leave. The book uses that premise in an argument about trustworthy guidance, not a vote-based source of authority.

blocks.question: Why is the vowel in mukhlas versus mukhlis important?
blocks.answer: The paper contrasts being purified by God with the active quality of sincerity. Similar transliterations must not erase the grammatical distinction.

modules.title: Difficult wording: tawriyah, reproach and Moses

references.title: New Religion question paper (highlighted choices, provenance unconfirmed)

blocks.text: When a narrative seems to conflict with infallibility, first identify what is actually alleged: deliberate falsehood, failure of an obligation, unintended consequence, a lawful act judged against a higher ideal, or an opponent’s accusation. The lesson does not treat those as interchangeable.

rows: Apparently untrue speech
Certain Abraham/Joseph narratives are explained through tawriyah in cited reports: intended meaning differs from the apparent meaning taken by a listener.
Not naskh (abrogation); not a blanket license for lying.
Prayers for forgiveness
Language can express humility, heightened spiritual standards or a departure from the better course.
Do not infer violation of an essential obligation from the word forgiveness alone.
Reproach / prohibition
The author considers audience, context and rhetorical function before inferring a committed sin.
A prohibition in an address is not itself proof that the addressed act occurred.
Special divine assistance
Increased means bring increased duties while action remains voluntary.
Assistance is not exemption from accountability.
Moses and the Qibti
The book says Moses struck once and the death was not intended.
Unintended death is not necessarily an accidental physical strike.

blocks.title: Q29 needs correction in your understanding
blocks.text: The paper highlights D, “an unintentional striking.” That is the closest intended option to the book’s explanation, but it is imprecise: the text describes a strike followed by an unintended death. Do not memorize “Moses accidentally moved his arm” or recast the story as a premeditated killing.

For Q27, the paper labels tawriyah “dissimulation.” Equivocation or an intended double meaning is more precise for the distinction being tested. The review reports the author’s reconciliation of these narratives; it does not claim that every interpretive school resolves them identically.

blocks.question: Someone calls tawriyah the cancellation of a previous religious rule. Correct the term.
blocks.answer: Cancellation or supersession is naskh, not tawriyah. Here tawriyah concerns intended versus apparent meaning in speech.

blocks.question: What two intentions must be kept separate in the Moses question?
blocks.answer: Intending a physical action and intending its fatal consequence. The source’s defense specifically denies an intended killing; the paper’s option collapses that distinction.

blocks.question: How should you analyze a new objection passage rather than memorize a stock response?
blocks.answer: Identify the action and obligation, the speaker’s perspective, intended outcome and context. Then check the book’s stated interpretation. Do not automatically label every difficult passage either deliberate sin or harmless metaphor.

modules.title: Opposition to prophets: who, why and how

references.title: New Religion question paper (highlighted choices, provenance unconfirmed)

blocks.text: Lesson 30 describes influential rulers and wealthy elites as frequent leaders of opposition in its account of prophetic history. It also describes early followers often drawn from people without power. These are patterns within the book’s account, not a claim that wealth by itself proves wrongdoing or that every individual belongs to one side.

rows: Who led?
Rulers and wealthy/influential groups in the cited examples.
Why resist?
Pride and self-interest; attachment to inherited customs; protection of wealth, rank and influence; desire to continue prohibited conduct.
Why might others follow?
Ignorance, deference to authorities, social pressure or coercion.
How was opposition expressed?
Mockery, slander, diversionary disputation, threats or inducements, and violence.
NOT a listed motive in Q33
Physical weakness.

blocks.text: Distinguish motive from method. Protecting income or status is a motive; publicly ridiculing a messenger is a method. Blindly repeating ancestral belief is not evidence that the belief is true simply because it is old. The same distinction helps with a new vignette that does not use the paper’s exact words.

blocks.question: A powerful person spreads accusations because reform threatens his income. Identify the motive and method separately.
blocks.answer: Motive: protecting economic advantage. Method: slander or discrediting the messenger. Neither is the same as an evidence-based rebuttal.

blocks.question: Why is “physical weakness” the odd option in Q33?
blocks.answer: The supplied list concerns moral, social and economic motives for resisting prophets, not bodily strength. The answer is limited to that list.

modules.title: Noah: separate the verse from the report

references.title: New Religion question paper (highlighted choices, provenance unconfirmed)
Bihar al-Anwar, vol. 11, part 3; reports attributed to Tafsir al-Ayyashi
references.locator: Numbered reports 56-57, Arabic and English displayed together; report provenance not independently authenticated

blocks.text: Hud 11:40 describes the flood sign, the instruction to embark, a stated family exception, and the small number who believed. It does not give an exact head count in that verse. For Q35, learn “few believers”; do not replace it with every towns-person, only animals, or an unsupported number.

rows: Q32: flood sign
B - water issuing from the oven (tannur), matching the cited report and the verse’s wording in this translation.
Learn the stated report, not every competing interpretation of tannur.
Q34: temporary stop
C is the marked and likely intended seal/signet answer. Al-Ayyashi report 57 describes a cover being placed and sealed, then opened.
The English rendering says seal; the paper calls it his ring. Do not imagine a ring alone plugging the opening.
Q35: passengers
A - few believers, along with the embarkation instructions and family exception in Hud 11:40.
The seal detail belongs to narration, not to this verse.

blocks.title: Source precision matters
blocks.text: Report 57 is explicitly attributed to Tafsir al-Ayyashi in the inspected compilation. This locates the narrative; it does not establish a hadith-authenticity verdict. Preserve the distinction between a source match, a translation choice and authentication.

blocks.question: Does finding the seal report prove that the Qur’anic verse itself mentions a ring?
blocks.answer: No. The verse and the later narrated detail are different sources.

modules.title: Religion, sharia, functions and guidance: keep the categories separate

references.title: Faith and Reason, Question 13: Non-Muslims and Hell

blocks.text: The paper repeatedly changes the level of classification. A definition of religion, its main content areas, its foundational beliefs and its practical branches are not four interchangeable lists. Start by identifying which list the stem asks for.

rows: Religion in this course
Divinely communicated beliefs and guidance, expressed through practical and moral requirements, directed toward human felicity.
A universal sociological definition that every tradition must accept.
Three content areas
Beliefs; practical commandments/orders; morals/values.
The three shared theological fundamentals: tawhid, prophethood and resurrection.
Sharia
Practical religious law governing conduct, duties and permitted/prohibited acts. D1 calls these secondary principles.
Secondary does not mean unimportant; beliefs and rituals alone are not the whole of sharia.
Din / al-din
The source cluster uses religion, recompense/reward and way/method. Context determines the intended sense.
Yawm al-din is the Day of Recompense/Judgment, not the literal expansion of din in every sentence.
Literal versus technical
Ordinary lexical usage versus a defined disciplinary meaning.
D31 is awkwardly laid out; it does not establish that every word necessarily has a distinct technical meaning.
External / internal guidance
Prophets and messengers are the outward guiding proof; intellect is the inward one in the cited tradition.
A claim that reasoning is dispensable, or that every intuition is prophetic revelation.

blocks.text: D17 illustrates why a concept is safer than memorizing a letter: the highlighted choice describes pulling someone away from a wrong path, whereas its answer sheet chooses guidance. These overlap as purpose and consequence. D24 has several near-synonymous lists of beliefs, rules and values, so it cannot reliably distinguish those answer letters.

rows: Explanatory / noetic
Makes a worldview intelligible: origin, purpose and ultimate destiny.
This is a useful analytic distinction, not a verified later-lecture heading.
Psychological
How meaning, trust, support and hope affect the believer’s experience.
A20 marks psychological; D25 also places meaningfulness under psychological function. Follow this course classification without claiming noetic and psychological are mutually exclusive.
Moral / social
Guidance for conduct, responsibility and relations with other people.
A comforting belief is not thereby proven true; a demanding belief is not thereby false.

blocks.text: D26 uses nihilism for the problem of meaninglessness. Its generalization is that suffering need not come only from poverty: someone may have resources yet lack purpose or support. This is a philosophical teaching point, not a diagnosis of everyone today, nor a claim that religious belief prevents mental illness. D23 gives the course’s religious account of felicity; D29 links purpose to meaning. Neither is a guarantee of wealth or an easy life.

blocks.title: Transfer rule
blocks.text: When a new question uses different wording, sort it first: definition -> content areas -> source of guidance -> function -> consequence. Do not answer a three-beliefs question with the three-content-areas list.

modules.title: Divine attributes and justice

references.title: Discursive Theology, Lesson 20 - definition attributed to Imam Ali

rows: Positive attributes
Affirm a perfection: knowledge, power and life.
Positive does not mean a flattering description selected at will.
Negative attributes
Deny a limitation or deficiency: ignorance, dependency or bodily composition.
Negative does not mean a bad quality possessed by God.
All-hearing / all-seeing
The intended course answer is knowledge of what is heard or seen, without dependence on human ears or eyes.
Avoid anthropomorphism, but do not erase the attribute altogether.
Essence / action
Life, knowledge and power characterize essence; creator and sustainer describe a relation to creatures.
This is a different classification from positive versus negative.

blocks.text: Justice concerns appropriate placement and due rights, not making every outcome identical. Distribution according to relevant need, right or capacity can exemplify justice; the criterion must be justified rather than assumed. Equal treatment in the relevant respect and different treatment in a genuinely different case need not conflict.

blocks.title: A real marked-answer problem: A11
blocks.text: A11 highlights D, distributing resources according to capacity. But B, putting everything in its place, is the more direct match for the saying attributed to Imam Ali and the broad definition explained by Yazdi. Learn both the definition and its possible application; retain the marked D as source evidence, not as a reason to redefine the term.

Generalization: distinguish the definition of justice, a distribution rule, the absence of oppression and a particular just action. A question can ask for any one of these. Theological claims in this section are presented in the course’s philosophical/Twelver framework, not as a statement that all schools formulate divine attributes identically.

modules.title: One revealed core, successive laws, final prophethood

blocks.text: The course uses Islam in two related senses: submission to the one God as the common revealed core, and the final dispensation brought by Muhammad. A stem that switches between these senses can become misleading. The course presents Moses and Jesus as genuine prophets, while holding that the final applicable dispensation is that of Muhammad.

rows: Revealed core
One God and divine guidance; the paper links unity to a shared human nature.
Different historical communities and languages.
Practical law
Guidance has concrete commands for the community addressed.
Some practical prescriptions across prophetic dispensations.
Abrogation / supersession
In this framework, later authorized law replaces earlier applicable law.
It does not mean every earlier prophet was false or every earlier moral truth disappears.
Universality
The final message addresses humanity rather than one ethnicity.
This is a claim about scope.
Finality
Muhammad is the seal of prophets; Quran is the final revelation in the paper’s formulation.
This is a claim about the end of prophethood, not the end of scholarship or guidance.

blocks.text: D59 tests the five ulu al-azm: Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus and Muhammad. Treat the five-name list as the course’s transmitted classification of major law-bearing prophets. It is not a list of every prophet, nor a proof that no other prophet received scripture. D7 links Moses with Judaism; D6 identifies the shared monotheistic claim. Christian Trinitarian belief should still be described on its own terms rather than mislabeled as simple polytheism.

blocks.title: Do not memorize contradictory keys
blocks.text: D11 selects both monotheism and polytheism, despite asking for the shared monotheistic foundation. D95 selects both the ending and continued validity of earlier laws without distinguishing foundational truth from current legal applicability. Those combined choices are not sound explanations.

D5’s wording about whether a person may call themselves a Jew confuses a communal identity with the theological obligation claimed by this course. Learn the intended claim about following genuine divine guidance when it is established, not an instruction to invalidate someone’s identity. D97 uses one God as the central belief; that is not a complete statement of every belief or legal condition associated with entering Islam.

The Arabic image in D100 was recovered and checked: it is Quran 3:85. The verse is used here for the course’s truth/finality claim. D99 invokes 2:256 on non-compulsion. A claimed obligation to believe, whether a proposition is true, and whether belief can be coerced are distinct questions; do not use one verse to erase the other.

modules.title: Pluralism, tolerance and salvation: three different claims

references.title: Faith and Reason, Question 13: Non-Muslims and Hell

rows: Truth
Whether conflicting religious doctrines are equally true.
Respectful treatment does not require agreeing with every doctrine.
Salvation
Whether and under what conditions people may be saved.
A theological truth claim alone does not establish the final judgment of each named individual.
Freedom / tolerance
How people may choose and how others should treat them.
Freedom of choice does not logically prove every available choice true.

blocks.text: D49/D88/D90 and A16 package pluralism as equal truth plus salvation across religions. Retain that as the simplified version being examined. It should not be treated as a precise definition of every philosophical pluralist theory, and salvation across traditions is not identical to saying every individual will be saved regardless of conduct.

The located Faith and Reason discussion distinguishes culpable refusal from inability to recognize the message. A person may never have encountered it adequately, or may have received a seriously distorted account. This is why merely hearing the name Islam is not enough to settle culpability. The course’s intermediate answer is some may be saved, some not; avoid blanket judgments of all outsiders.

rows: No fair access / no capacity
Accountability must consider what someone could actually understand and choose.
Source-supported qualification, not a personal verdict.
Informed, deliberate rejection
The course distinguishes this from innocent ignorance.
Do not infer a real individual’s intentions from their religious label.
Post-death testing
D3 and D12 select a later test for the ignorant.
Retained as the paper’s reported teaching; its exact hadith and scope were not established here.
Contradictory truth claims
A proposition and its exact negation cannot both be true in the same respect.
This logical point by itself is not a complete refutation of all pluralism or a rule about every person’s destiny.

blocks.text: D96 and D98 are compressed polemical items, not full arguments. D98 even offers near-identical negative options. The transferable skill is to distinguish contradiction in propositions from diversity among people, and doctrinal disagreement from denial of civil respect.

blocks.title: Worked distinction
blocks.text: “I disagree that two contradictory claims are both true” does not entail “I know the eternal fate of everyone who holds the other view.” Truth, access to evidence, intention, conduct and judgment are separate steps.

modules.title: Faith, practice, intention and degrees
modules.basis: D19-20,D53,D91-93; integrated with earlier responsibility teaching

blocks.text: The paper treats faith as something strengthened in practice rather than merely pronounced. Keep belief, willing commitment and outward action distinguishable. Knowing a claim, assenting to it, and living in accordance with it are related but not identical.

rows: Iman / faith
Inward believing commitment with consequences for conduct.
A label or isolated verbal declaration is not a measurement of inward sincerity.
Practice
Repeated conduct aligned with what is believed.
D20 offers practice and action separately even though they overlap. The intended teaching is reinforcement through living the belief.
Niyyah / niya
Intention: what the person aims at in acting.
Ikhlas is sincerity/purity of intention, not the literal translation of niyyah.
Degrees of faith
People can differ in strength and maturity of commitment.
D91 does not imply unequal human dignity.
Ten-rung image
D92 attributes ten degrees, like a ladder, to Imam Jafar al-Sadiq.
Record it as the transmitted teaching being tested; this review does not authenticate the hadith chain.
Highest degree
D93 names the Prophet and his household in its Twelver framework.
Not a license to grade the unseen state of ordinary individuals.

blocks.title: D19 remains a real source gap
blocks.text: The compilation marks three stages, but does not name them. Its separate ten-degree ladder item is a different formulation. Do not invent three names or silently substitute three degrees of certainty; the relevant lecture is needed.

A useful model for revision is belief -> intention -> chosen conduct -> reinforcement or weakening of habits. The direction also runs back from repeated conduct to the strength of commitment. This is a teaching relationship, not a claim that a single lapse automatically extinguishes all faith.

Compare two outwardly similar actions with different intentions, and two people who say the same sentence but act differently. The paper’s point is to assess the inner aim and practical commitment alongside the act, rather than treating faith as a fixed label or worldly success as proof of sincerity.

modules.title: This world and the Hereafter: aim, action and consequence

headers: This life in the course account
rows: Duration
Temporary and passing.
Enduring, not simply another brief stage of earthly life.
Role
Opportunity for choice, action and cultivation.
Disclosure, judgment and consequences of what was cultivated.
Metaphor
Bridge / field in which one plants.
Destination / harvest; not a second, more complicated introduction.
Practical implication
Present acts and responsibilities matter.
Long-term accountability changes how immediate gain is evaluated.

blocks.text: A17 combines duration and the ability to change one’s course through action. D52 rejects the idea that the Hereafter is merely a more complicated introductory world. The generalization is not that this life is worthless: something can be a means and still matter profoundly because it shapes the outcome.

Apply the distinction to a tempting short-term benefit obtained by harming someone else. The lesson asks the student to evaluate responsibility and ultimate consequence, not just immediate pleasure. Similarly, hardship now does not by itself demonstrate ultimate failure, and prosperity now does not establish moral worth.

blocks.title: Do not overextend the contrast
blocks.text: These metaphors concern the course’s account of moral action and judgment. They are not a complete treatment of barzakh, intercession or every question about the afterlife; those require their own evidence.

modules.title: Prophetic biography: childhood and family

references.title: Ja'far Subhani, The Message - Chapter 7: Rejoining the Family
The Message - Chapter 9: From Sheperd to Merchant

rows: Birth
Muhammad; Mecca; approximately 570 CE in D34.
A conventional course chronology, not a precisely established modern birth certificate.
Abdullah
Father; paper places his death before Muhammad’s birth.
Keep father distinct from grandfather and guardian uncle.
Aminah
Mother; paper gives her death when he was six.
Subhani’s account places her death at Abwa on the return from Yathrib.
Halimah
Foster mother; paper gives return to Aminah after five years.
Subhani chapter 7 supports this version; ages in biographical traditions need source labels.
Abdul Muttalib -> Abu Talib
Grandfather’s care, then guardianship by the uncle.
Abu Talib is not the father or grandfather.
Khadijah
Wife, first woman accepting the message in the paper, mother of Fatimah; honored in traditions.
D38 gives marriage age forty. Subhani explicitly notes reports of a lower age as well.

blocks.text: Learn relationships as well as chronology: Abdullah/Aminah are parents; Halimah is foster mother; Abdul Muttalib is grandfather; Abu Talib is uncle and guardian; Khadijah is wife and Fatimah’s mother. This prevents an unfamiliar wording from breaking a memorized list.

blocks.title: D43: related narrative found, wording not authenticated
blocks.text: The compilation calls the person a physiognomist and marks a warning about Jews. Subhani chapter 7 contains a related warning in the story of Bahira, a Christian monk, during the Syrian journey. That is a match to a narrated episode, not proof of the paper’s exact occupational label, not verification of supernatural prediction, and never grounds for a generalization about Jewish people.

modules.title: Revelation, public invitation and migration

references.title: The Message - Chapter 12: The First Revelation

rows: Revelation
D39 lists inspiration, dreams and encounter with Gabriel as spiritual communication forms.
An ordinary dream or intuition does not itself certify prophethood.
First revelation / mission
D40 uses initial verses of al-Alaq (chapter 96), Gabriel and 27 Rajab.
Subhani chapter 12 identifies 27 Rajab as the Shi‘i mission-date tradition and discusses Ramadan reports. Preserve this qualification.
Early -> public invitation
D41 gives three years; D46 gives about forty followers.
An approximate traditional count is not a universal historical census.
Warning near relatives
Quran 26:214 is associated in these papers with public invitation; D86 calls the family episode Yawm al-dar.
Do not confuse it with the later Hijrah conspiracy meeting.
Narrator/compiler
D87 selects Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari for the Yawm al-dar report.
A later compiler is not an eyewitness; exact passage/authentication remains to be established.
Dar al-Nadwah
Council location of Quraysh in the migration/conspiracy questions.
It is not the cave used for refuge.
Ali / Thawr
A9/F15: Ali sleeps in the Prophet’s bed. D80: refuge in Thawr.
Thawr belongs to the Hijrah narrative; Hira is associated with retreat/revelation.

blocks.text: Keep three episodes separate: invitation to relatives, wider public preaching, and the plot preceding migration. Learn event -> location -> person -> purpose. Several questions test exactly this reversal rather than a new doctrine.

blocks.title: D79 and D85 must not be collapsed
blocks.text: D85 describes an old man as Satan in the tradition. D79 separately marks Satan as the proposer of the multi-tribe killing plan. Being the visitor or approver is not automatically being the proposer. The exact course narrative has not been established sufficiently to certify D79; keep this flagged rather than convert the marked choice into historical fact.

D55 gives completing ethical virtues as a purpose of prophets. Its other choices also overlap genuine religious aims, so it is a weak single-answer discriminator. The useful idea is that prophetic guidance includes moral and social conduct, not information about the unseen alone.

modules.title: Scripture literacy: books, commandments and common figures

rows: Bible divisions
The Christian Bible has Old and New Testaments.
D64’s two Bibles is imprecise. Two main divisions are not two separate rival Bibles; traditions differ in canon.
Pentateuch / Torah
Genesis -> Exodus -> Leviticus -> Numbers -> Deuteronomy.
D65 asks this order. Traditional Mosaic attribution is not a resolved claim about modern historical authorship.
Ten Commandments
Associated with Moses; found in Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5.
Not a list issued first to Abraham, Jesus or Muhammad.
Decalogue recognition
Exclusive worship; restrictions on images/idolatry and misuse of the divine name; Sabbath; honoring parents; prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft, false witness and coveting.
Numbering/grouping varies. D63’s generic command to pray is not one of the listed formulations.
Golden calf
D62: Moses returns to find the people worshipping a calf.
The specific object of disobedience matters, not only the vague word bad.
Abraham
D50 tests the biblical association of the name with father of many nations.
Identify the narrative meaning without pretending all etymological questions are settled by an English mnemonic.
Parents
Honor of parents appears in the Decalogue and Quranic teaching, including 17:23.
This is shared ethical content, not evidence that the two texts are identical.

blocks.text: For Pharaoh, A2/D48 tests the explicit preservation of his body in Quran 10:92. Distinguish preservation of the body as a sign from spiritual salvation. The comparison with Exodus concerns that specific detail; it is not a claim that the Bible has no Pharaoh narrative. Nor does the verse alone identify a particular surviving mummy.

blocks.title: Maurice Bucaille: retain the name, qualify the biography
blocks.text: A14/F18 intends Maurice Bucaille, the French physician/writer associated with Quran-and-Bible comparisons. The selected option adds conversion to Islam. No reliable first-person conversion evidence was established in this pass, so that clause is not taught as verified biography.

modules.title: Jesus, Mary and prediction claims: compare without conflating

rows: Jesus in the New Testament
Crucifixion, then resurrection on the third day.
Resurrection and ascension are different events; Acts 1 describes appearances over forty days before the ascension scene. D78 conflates them.
Jesus in Quran 4:157-158
His opponents did not kill/crucify him; God raised him.
The passage does not explicitly name a substitute. D69 gives a substitution interpretation, not the verbatim content of the verse.
Mary in the Quran
Chosen and chaste; D67.
This does not imply every Biblical portrayal is insulting.
Mary in the Bible
D66 marks a normal and insulting portrayal.
Luke 1:28 and 1:42 honor Mary. The blanket insult claim is unsupported and should not be memorized as fact.
Comforter / Paraclete
D60 and A6 connect it to Muhammad in the course’s apologetic reading.
Parakletos means advocate/helper/comforter, not praised. John 14:26 identifies the Advocate with the Holy Spirit.
Ahmad
Quran 61:6 describes Jesus announcing a messenger named Ahmad.
This is the Quranic passage. It is not a lexical translation of parakletos.
Deuteronomy 18:18
D70 intends Muhammad for a prophet like Moses.
The verse does not explicitly name him. Its Israelite-prophetic context and Christian messianic reception differ from this Muslim interpretation.

blocks.text: For any comparison, write three labels mentally: what the text says; how a tradition interprets it; what the paper expects. These can overlap without being identical. A correct attribution is more precise than pretending that all traditions agree or that an interpretation is a literal translation.

blocks.title: D77 is unsafe as a clean discriminator
blocks.text: The paper says both Muhammad and Moses brought Islam, elsewhere using Islam for shared submission, but here marks that very similarity as incorrect. It also calls their ministers brothers without distinguishing biological kinship from religious brotherhood. The stem changes senses; learn the distinctions instead of treating the supplied letter as an uncontested fact.

modules.title: Guidance after the Prophet: Thaqalayn and authority

blocks.text: Thaqalayn is the tradition of the two weighty/precious things. In this course the paired references are the Quran and the Ahl al-Bayt, the Prophet’s household. The repeated question directions are: name the tradition, name the pair, and explain the guidance role after the Prophet.

blocks.title: Correct the repeated typo
blocks.text: The papers repeatedly say after the demise of the Holy Quran. The intended person is the Holy Prophet; the Quran is the text people are told to hold to. Leaving the typo uncorrected changes the meaning of the statement.

The course’s Twelver use of the tradition links scriptural guidance to the Prophet’s household and its authority in interpretation. That is distinct from receiving a new prophetic scripture. Yazdi’s appointment-of-an-Imam discussion provides relevant doctrinal context, while the status and interpretation of individual reports require their own scholarly treatment.

D82 gives a vague statement about struggles and differences after the Prophet’s death. It signals a succession/authority theme but supplies no named event or chronology. This review does not manufacture a detailed later lecture or a separate historical answer from that vague stem.

A8/F20 asks what is not a sign of religious truth: number of followers. Popularity is a sociological observation, not a logical demonstration. Likewise, merely asserting an earlier prediction is not enough; the text, interpretation and evidence must be checked. Keep evidence for authority distinct from the headcount of supporters.

modules.title: Religious ethics and the medical items: learn the conditions

references.title: Sistani - Medical questions, examination and autopsy

blocks.title: Study context, not a clinical or legal protocol
blocks.text: These questions mix moral teachings and religious legal rulings. The exact lecturer’s jurist and edition were not supplied. The checked Sistani rulings below are a named comparison, not a claim that every jurist or civil legal system gives the same answer. Real care requires current local law, clinical standards and supervision.

rows: D71 - marriage priorities
The paper emphasizes faith/character rather than choosing only for wealth or appearance.
Its attributed reward of both money and beauty is not a guaranteed outcome; exact narration/authority remains unverified.
D72 - dissection
Consent, purpose and necessity are distinct considerations.
The marked choice says personal willingness alone is insufficient. The paper also assumes research broadly permits dissection, which cannot be generalized from the checked rulings.
D73 - examination
A necessity exception must remain proportionate to the needed examination.
Revealing more than required is the tested problem. Necessary area, available alternatives, looking and touching must be considered separately.
D74 - ethics and work
Paper associates righteous conduct with a way out of hardship.
Its unclear phrasing does not establish an exact verse or promise of automatic financial success.
D75 - opposing oppression
The quoted saying teaches opposing the oppressor and helping the oppressed.
Use this concrete moral direction, not only the broad wording caring about affairs.
D76 - injector liability
Qualification, care, permission, release from liability and cause of harm are different variables.
The paper’s no responsibility answer is conditional; consent alone is not universal immunity.

blocks.text: The official Sistani comparison is narrower than the paper’s shorthand: the medical Q&A limits exposure to examination needs; the physician-liability rulings distinguish a release from liability and competent, careful treatment; the dissection ruling does not give blanket permission for routine educational dissection of a Muslim merely because it is useful. Do not turn D72 or D76 into a universal rule.

blocks.title: A reusable decision structure
blocks.text: Identify the act -> identify the authority and jurisdiction -> state permission/necessity -> limit scope -> check competence and precaution -> consider harm and responsibility. Omitting a condition can reverse the answer.

D54 needs a separate history correction: Socrates was an ancient Greek philosopher, not a medieval theologian. Erasmus is associated with Christian humanism, so the paper’s claim that his humanist ideals do not fit Christianity is also misleading. More than one option is problematic; it is not safe to learn a sweeping account of liberalism from this item. The review retains this as a flagged comparison topic, not a newly verified core textbook chapter.

options.D: A conscious and rational rejection of the concept of God.
